text: This story is very cool, and it’s exciting to see how much progress AI will bring to every field. One thing to temper everyone from wanting to lidar the whole world is human capacity. Finding discoveries like this is essentially as hard as doing the lidar mapping. Now the issue will be getting archaeologist there in time before someone else does. The best way to protect a site is to leave it alone. If we start finding dozens or hundreds of sites it will be more than what archaeologists can excavate and protest. Treasure hunters and looters don’t care about stratigraphy and the processes involved for doing research. Maybe the cat is out of the bag on this one, but good for thought. Edit: I’m not saying we shouldn’t have people use AI to do this or that no bad actor will. This comment is in response to the sentiment I am seeing in the comments that we should lidar the whole world and have AI find any anomalous structures it can. There is no way for archeologists to excavate and protect all those places in that scenario

text: Show HN: Klad, a paint app your coding agent can drive (source-available). I've been developing applications for a long time and have turned to game development as well lately. One of the things that frustrated me the most was that using AI agents for game development is very annoying in the art department. Your only options right now are to either use an image genAI model and roll the dice every time you want to make an edit, or have your agent draw with something like vectors. I was looking for an application that would allow me to ask an agent to make a first draft of whatever art I needed with actual brushes, and then be able to go in myself and edit every last stroke or layer that it created. Klad is that application. Written in Rust, it can be fully controlled by an agent through the CLI, and every function is available in a nice UI as well: a brush engine, frame-by-frame animation (and bones/IK), vectors, text layers, colours, layer effects, infinite undo (even after re-opening the file!),… Why I think it's useful for a wider audience: Adobe showed agents editing Photoshop files at MAX this week, with a private beta planned for early 2027. Klad is built on the same core idea, with editable paint strokes as core architecture, and it works today. Clone the repo to try it out: https://github.com/klad-app/klad You can basically point Claude to the repo, ask it to build it, and pick up the drawing skills. Then ask it to make any drawing you want! (After that, you or the agent can change absolutely every brush stroke in the app again, which makes edits a breeze.) The quality of the drawings really depends on the agent you use. I have tried it with Claude Fable 5.2 since it came out on Monday, and the drawings are already quite impressive. I'm confident that this will only improve. I use it every day on Mac, so that definitely works well. It builds on Linux too (tablet pen pressure still needs some work there). Windows builds in CI, I haven't used it there myself yet but I have some reports that it works perfectly fine. Coming up next is support for pixel art. I'm in the testing phase with this right now, and I expect it to go live in the repo sometime this weekend. Klad is source-available rather than open source: free to build and use for individuals and small companies, and I plan to sell pre-built binaries later, the way Aseprite does. The file format, CLI reference and agent skill are MIT. What I want to hear from people who try it: Can your agent work out the CLI without help, and where does it get confused? Can you go in and change one of its strokes easily? The command reference and guides are available at https://klad.studio I'll be here answering any questions about the technical side as well, as it's a pretty interesting challenge to build a performant engine with editable brush strokes that render as paint.

Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings. Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer. As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman. I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy. To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp). I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use. Would love to hear what you think about the onboarding and note taking experience :)

As attacks on infrastructure grow more powerful, our goal is to bring state-of-the-art defenses to individuals and organizations as quickly as possible, without making them trade away performance or ease of use. Our mission[1] is to create a private garden for thought, where people keep control of their own agency, and we keep evolving our research[2] to stay ahead of rapidly changing threat models. Experience deploying software in regulated industries (finance, cybersecurity, government, biotech) or guiding customers through security reviews 3. Experience with model serving or inference infrastructure 4. Public technical writing or speaking We encourage you to apply even if you don’t meet every single qualification! text: EventQL seems nice, but > While an EventQL precondition is evaluated, every other write waits, so that nothing can come in between; reads go on meanwhile. So that no write holds up the others for long, the EventQL preconditions of a write are evaluated for at most five seconds, all of them together, counted from when the write gets its turn: a write whose preconditions take longer is rejected, with nothing written, with a 400 (From https://www.eventfoundation.io/docs/eventsourcingdb/precondi... ) That seems like a huge foot gun. Like, sure, you don't have to implement transactional semantics or think about consistency/MVCC/snapshots. But at the cost of "every UPDATE ... WHERE prevents every other write for up to 5 seconds"? Really? That seems like a bad tradeoff, inferior to both (massive effort) implementing proper transactionality, (medium efffort, but significantly compatibility-breaking) removing support for hierarchically-nested subjects so that the global-mutex restrictions on UPDATE-WHERE can be lifted/efficiently scoped to a subject, or (lowest effort) removing support for EventQL preconditions entirely. In any sufficiently large/multi-developer system I don't imagine that "don't use EventQL preconditions" will effectively stick. As it is, I feel like having the main event sourcing system blocked for up to 5sec on any one client's slow EventQL precondition is asking for pervasive downtime events out of nowhere. That said, I may be missing something that ameliorates those issues! I'm just skimming docs, so take it with a grain of salt.

text: I have been trying for a while to put irregular things (point clouds) in regular grids, to use the grid itself as a data structure. Not because it is better, but just because grids are more structured than e.g. trees and thus easier integrate into ML pipelines. It all started here, with simple multi-indexing: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49042861 Then I realised that to make the multi-indexing procedure more effective, I need some kind of preprocessing, to make the points flat (2d insteed of 3d). When they are already flat I can sort them better. Then I heard about mesh flattening, https://geometrycollective.github.io/boundary-first-flatteni... geometry images https://hhoppe.com/proj/gim/ and thought: this is something I need to try with point clouds, whenever they have a latent surfacic distribution. And well, it seems to work. At least now I can have bunnys dragon and elephants all to fit in the grid and not getting half of the legs, ears or whatever lost in the process.

text: We have been building GFQL for open source vectorized CPU/GPU cypher on dataframes (think duckdb for graphs, no DB needed) using agentic assistance... and our thinking is this is a stepping stone to something even more aggressive Today, we embrace optimizing hotpath specializations for some patterns that would have been too expensive to maintain before. LLMs keep that cost bearable, and being able to do that for important users (like users of our analyst product Graphistry) is a superpower. Our scores on graph community benchmarks are beating the big guys - and importantly, on anything we care about. Where we really want that to go is runtime / loadtime specialization. Our customers would absolutely want their top queries autotuned. DB research is already heavily tilting here, akin to tracing compiler research a decade ago. I'm quite bullish on what is now possible.

text: There has been a similar issue in the GPU-kernel dev community. It was solved by understanding that the value provided by the benchmarks depends on your use-case. It sounds like the author in the article is yelling at the benchmark from his own idea of what a DB search should be (reliable, general), and not from what the benchmark is measuring. If you just want the fastest kernel for a handful of shapes, let people make brittle but fast code. If you are interested in general broad solutions, benchmark 50 different entries, limit code size to disallow assembly branches for every possible entry. Put requirements like bitwise equivalence or other end-task limits in there. Have public & private datasets. I think it's more of a proof that we should spend more time thinking about what and why we want these things, and design benchmarks that reflect that instead of going of the old way of doing things.

text: I use a kei truck for farming. They are incredibly pragmatic little vehicles. They are very capable driving around on dirt/gravel agricultural roads with 4WD, and they are inexpensive and robust enough that you can really beat them up and use them as a tool without worry. Repairs and replacement parts are ubiquitous and inexpensive. Having the sides of bed fold down is also really useful. They aren't comfortable to drive at all (although just having A/C at all on a hot summer day in the field is a godsend), and I wouldn't want to do longer trips in one - although you certainly could in a pinch. It seems like Toyota/Scion is just testing the waters here, and I'm not sure how successful they'll be. But I hope there is a future for kei trucks in the US.

text: I feel like I am commenting this under every post mentioning fingerprinting, but is there a technical reason access to fingerprinting information (screen resolution, battery level, etc) couldn't be made to "taint" the data/code, where the browser would then refuse to send off that data? Or anonymise it and replay the code before sending the request. Of course, there are legitimate use-cases: downloading specific assets based on client device, etc. And that's a whole can of worms of side channels to open, but that would feel like a useful additional layer of defense, and the paranoia level could be configured. The price might be subtle bugs, and/or a permission dialog that most people will ignore. I am asking this as, from what I've seen, most websites do not need complex interactions: the battery level will be used to render a battery indicator, etc. XHRs do not usually depend on such data.

text: Show HN: Black Ops II statically recompiled to native ARM64 macOS. I grew up with Black Ops 2 and wanted to see if I could make it work on my 2020 MacBook Pro. So I used Claude Opus 5.5 to create a tool that converts your copy of the game (from Steam) to a native ARM64 Mac app, with almost 60fps in all areas. The whole game is statically recompilated ahead-of-time (AOT) and does not use any emulator whatsoever, be it Wine, Crossover or Rosetta. The best thing is the performance, although some heat issues are still to fix. You get to play the whole Campaign, local Multiplayer (with bots) and local Zombies (all DLCs maps; you need to have them in your Steam library obviously) at about 60fps. Split-screen was not in the PC version, but I've been working on it lately; it's coming soon! LAN mode is on the roadmap for later too :)

text: I've used to same technique to get Fallout: New Vegas running on Asahi Linux on MacOS. Its quite a step, but https://github.com/doitsujin/dxvk makes it possible to skip a lot of work and get the game running in day. You can then make any changes you want, so I'm running fallout nv on a wide display in native resolution and some graphical improvements. Realtime whole world shadow maps, SSAO, tonemap + color grading, FXAA and Hor+ FOV. Gives me a solid 60fps most of the time, with only the occasianal bug here and there that is often fixed in no time. Luckily i've added 10min auto save quite quickly, so that it does not cause that big of a problem. Aside from the fun of both getting the game to work on this machine, and the fun of actually being able to play the game, it is a great way to find creative ways to work with LLM. Building out dev tools on the way that works for an LLM etc.
